name: Baking makeup technique

lead: Baking is a makeup technique in which a generous layer of loose translucent powder is pressed onto areas of liquid or cream makeup, usually under the eyes, along the cheekbones and down the nose, and left to sit before the excess is brushed away.

Practitioners use it to make concealer and foundation look smoother, set them for longer wear, and create a bright, sharply defined finish. It is closely tied to contouring and highlighting and is popular in stage, drag and social-media makeup.

paras: People apply concealer, press loose powder over chosen areas with a puff or sponge, wait for the heat of the skin to set it, then dust off the excess with a brush. It is typically followed by other face makeup.

The finish can look heavy or emphasise dry patches and fine lines on some skin. Dermatologists generally advise removing makeup thoroughly; people with sensitive or acne-prone skin sometimes report irritation.

chain: Set it under a layer of loose powder
angle.text: Baking changes how the skin looks by setting makeup so it creases less and reads brighter and more matte. It is used by people who wear makeup for a polished, defined finish, including for photography and performance.

lead: Baking is a makeup technique in which a thick layer of translucent powder is left on top of cream or liquid makeup, usually under the eyes and on the high points of the face, so that the base sets before the excess powder is brushed away. [1] It is used to give a matte, poreless-looking finish that lasts under hot lights and flash photography, and to brighten the under-eye area and sharpen contour and highlight. [1]

Makeup artists describe several appearance uses: setting concealer so it creases less, softening the look of dark circles, absorbing facial oil, catching eyeshadow fallout that can be swept away, and giving contour and highlight crisper edges. [1] Makeup artist Jamie Greenberg places baking under the umbrella of contouring. [1]

The technique is described as an old one with roots in stage and drag makeup. Its profile grew through RuPaul's Drag Race, YouTube tutorials and Instagram, which turned it into a widely used beauty term. [1] No clinical studies have examined baking itself.

paras: Baking layers translucent powder over base makeup. The powder is left in place for a few minutes, during which it absorbs oil and the warmth of the skin helps the base set, and is then brushed off. [1] The areas treated are typically the under-eyes and the high points of the face: cheekbones, nose bridge, chin and forehead. [1]
Makeup artists commonly concentrate the technique under the eyes, where the skin is dry and sensitive. [1]

Performers and models use baking to reduce touch-ups under stage lighting and flash. [1] It is also used as a non-shimmery highlight, to set highlighter, and to sharpen the edges of a contour. [1] Special-effects makeup artists are reported to use a similar approach to set bruises and cuts, though this is not well documented. [1]

Accounts describe baking as a very old makeup technique, with stage and drag performers using extra powder to keep eye makeup in place and make the under-eye area stand out under intense lighting. [1] It reached a wider audience through RuPaul's Drag Race, where contestants use it while preparing, and through bloggers and vloggers on YouTube and Instagram, where it became a widely used beauty buzzword. [1] Season 7 contestant Miss Fame is cited as one performer who demonstrated it in tutorials. [1]

Baking is usually discussed alongside contouring, which has a longer history that runs from Elizabethan stage makeup and greasepaint through Max Factor's film makeup in the 1930s and 1940s, Kevyn Aucoin's sculpted looks in the 1990s, and the social-media contour trend of the 2010s. [2]

Many makeup artists say baking is not well suited to ageing skin, because heavy powder can settle into fine lines and emphasise dryness; users counter that it is used under the eyes specifically to stop concealer from creasing in lines. [1] Heavy application can also look cakey, which is why some people use a lighter hand or restrict it to small areas. [1]

Baking belongs to the makeup and style end of appearance discussion, where it is used by people who wear makeup for photos, events or performance. The looksmaxxing community divides practices into softmaxxing, which covers non-invasive changes such as skincare, grooming, clothing and fitness, and harder interventions such as surgery. [3]

timeline.event: Elizabethan stage actors use chalk and soot to make expressions readable, an early ancestor of stage contouring. [2]
Max Factor Sr. adds shading to film makeup so faces do not look flat on screen. [2]
Kevyn Aucoin's book Face Forward popularises sculpting and contouring. [2]
Contouring and powder-setting techniques spread through RuPaul's Drag Race, YouTube and Instagram. [1][2]
